Casson explains that when Alexandria was a brand-new city in the third century BC, its founders enticed intellectuals to the city—in an attempt to establish it as a cultural center—with the famous museum, “a figurative temple for the muses, a place for cultivating the arts they symbolized. It was an ancient version of a think-tank: the members, consisting of noted writers, poets, scientists, and scholars, were appointed by the Ptolemies for life and enjoyed a handsome salary, tax exemption . . . free lodging, and food. . . . It was for them that the Ptolemies founded the library of Alexandria” (33–34).
